newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma to run for second term in 3 years.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma to run for second term in 3 years.

text.p: Ukraine's President Leonid Kuchma said on Monday that he intended to run for a second term in office -- more than three years ahead of scheduled presidential elections.

"So much needs to be done to reform the economy that one term is not enough," Kuchma told Ukraine's private Gravis television channel. "Ten years is the minimum period for a country which has launched radical reforms to achieve results."
Extracts of the interview were released ahead of broadcast by Interfax Ukraine news agency.
Kuchma remains Ukraine's most popular politician after being elected in July 1994 on a platform of forging closer ties with Russia.
He ousted Ukraine's first post-Soviet president, Leonid Kravchuk, in the first peaceful transfer of power from one president to another in a former Soviet republic.
Kuchma has since proved to be a stauncher defender of national interests than Kravchuk, winning the support of even ardent nationalists in western Ukraine.
He also ended two years of inaction in pursuing market-oriented change, sponsoring a reform programme that won the backing of Western financial institutions.
But results have been mixed, with the economy continuing to contract and millions still below the poverty line.
Under Ukraine's constitution approved in June, the president can serve for two five-year terms and the next elections are scheduled for October 1999.

Kuchma's statement could be aimed at warning potential rivals -- including current Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko as well as his predecessor -- that he would tolerate no campaign against his administration.

Ukrainian media have recently said that politics has been reduced to conflicts between "clans" representing corporate and other interests -- particularly in the country's two most influential industrial regions of Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.

In his interview, Kuchma appeared to acknowledge the clash of interests, appealing for development of an independent press "which does not serve various clans reflecting the activities of political parties...but defends the thinking of the majority of the people".
